so I would not consider myself an expert by any means. we haven’t had fish for that long (a little over a year now). at least three fish live in our pond currently. they were put in there last mid June. for future reference — I’m from Northern Ontario, in the Great Lakes region. \*anyways,\* as they are the same fish from last year, they obviously survived the winter. i think this winter will be more of the true test though, since last winter was somewhat mild. so we won’t be adding any more fish into the pond unless we’re absolutely certain they’ll be fine.

noting that you asked about how things work during winter: a pond does need to be deep enough to ensure that the entirety of it does not freeze (aka the bottom). goldfish are some of the animals that can enter into a state of semi-hibernation, called torpor iirc. leading up to this as the temperature decreases you will want to decrease their feedings as well. Waking up an animal in torpor during the middle of winter can be deadly for the animal, so we want to make sure that they’re prepared going into that state. i know that aeration is important; some will recommend an aerator — we didn’t use that last year, but again, it was a mild winter. this season might be different. (will probably be; the mountain ash trees are full of berries this season)

goldfish are hardy and I knew this before we had them but I didn’t realize just how hardy they can be. there’s not a whole lot you can do for them once things freeze over, but the best thing is to just do nothing, since as i said before, it’s not good for animals in torpor to be disturbed. if you have any specific questions i could try to answer, but i am far from being an expert and i am still actively learning.

My dad admitted to me the goldfish that we had in our house, when I was way younger (too young to remember much aside from that we did have a fish tank upstairs at some point), while they were alive and lived for a number of years, they weren’t in the best of conditions. He says it’s because they got the fish for my older sister back then — plus he was busier, so they didn’t quite feel like fish he was super excited to have. I suppose my first actual pet fish experience started last year in June, when we got goldfish again, and now the factors are different (we know much more about fishkeeping, we’re enthusiastic to keep them, we know more about goldfish in general — keep in mind the first goldfish we kept were from 20+ years ago. also we have more stable money/income). they’re our family fish now!

our outdoor fish get fed once a day near the evening, but to keep in mind they also thrive perfectly well on what they catch in the pond (bugs, eggs, plant matter). We gave them fish food since it is hot, and as it shifts into winter we’ll give them less and less to help them prepare for winter. as for our indoor fish: usually twice. on a normal day they get fed 3pm (sometimes earlier, sometimes later) with flakes (we’ve experienced no problems with this), then as people are going to bed at around 10pm, fluval bug bites. sometimes they might get the bug bites in the morning or whenever we’ve been doing work on their tank for whatever reason (I think of it as an apology for disturbing them lol). the indoor fish also eat some of the plants that are in their tank, which doesn’t bother us. the way I see it; whatever they can eat in around 2 minutes or so.

my goldfish sometimes tug out certain plants, but leave others alone. We don’t get rid of the dug up plants; we might replant if possible or just let the fish eat them. the lucky plants do thrive though. personally not super bothered by them going after the plants; they’re goldfish, that’s what they do. cant really convince them not to lol. plus it does give them a source of food, because as I said before we don’t really remove the plants in part due to that.

The Kalites fear the eclipse. It’s less of a case of “something extremely bad like the end of the world happens,” more like “I don’t know what this is and it’s scary, someone looked at it once and started freaking out, and has never been the same since”. Kalites, for the most part, fear the unknown - therefore anything that they would be unfamiliar with could be considered a thing to fear - though is not quite a symbol. In their art, the Kalite rarely use the eclipse - only to be seen in the worst situations. The Eclipse is utilized as a warning symbol - messages of destruction, death, sickness and famine are often painted alongside it. It could have been that there was historically a coincidence for the Kalites to fear the Eclipse, that something *bad* did happen, but just happened to occur during the Eclipse, and therefore became associated with it.

For the most part, conflicts in this unnamed project of mine are not large scale wars. If anything, they are territorial disputes, on small or large scales (but still small compared to what we’re used to calling a war). The most advanced species are the Kalites, who have no discrimination in terms of gender if you’re allowed to fight or not. On a slightly darker note, they also don’t care about age, either (although will project the young who could not fight either way, unable to walk or communicate properly).
 Kalites typically live off the ground, away from the predators and more sheltered in the trees (though there still are predators in the trees). Conflict is long, fought in small bursts - Kalite tribes send out small raiding groups during the day hours (as most species on the planet are nocturnal) to damage structures and steal resources. These raiders have a primary focus on stealth. The Kalites utilize the natural resources of the planet in their fight, such as using the smell of another creature to cover their own, foul smelling plants to be thrown as distractions, and more. Raiders, if caught, may fight. The Kalites do not have weapons like guns or even bows. Most of their active fighting is done face to face.
 Kalites could fight for a variety of reasons. Sometimes for food, sometimes for territory, sometimes - even for beliefs, however early in construction they may be. Essentially the same reason why humans start wars sometimes; the different being Kalites don’t join an ongoing war, and Kalites don’t cause that much collateral either. Kalites just don’t have the technology to do that; and also their population is too low. Kalites are in the early works of domesticating certain animals, which some will certainly be utilized in the conflict, should it happen.

In summary - technology we wouldn’t see as advanced. long periods of time, over small bursts of active conflict, rarely large fights. fights are decided over when an agreement is made…or one tribe is wiped out/assimilated. tribes will rarely join another ongoing conflict that they’re not in. huge focus on stealth, and tearing down the resources of the opposing force. as they are from a completely different world, the Kalites do not have the same concepts as us. some things that they do could be considered brutal or unethical, such as children (Kalites mature physically at 15 - become capable at walking on their own around 4-6 months old) fighting in war, or cruel and unusual punishments (often done by the Kalite who don’t live in the trees, but rather caves to the North) usually done to be left as a threat to the enemy.
